title: Unit 3b - Classes: Title Slide
summary: Title slide introducing Unit 3b on Classes in C++ for CS 103, presented by Mark Redekopp.
main_text: This is the title slide for Unit 3b of CS 103, covering the topic of Classes in C++. The unit is presented by Mark Redekopp. Classes are a fundamental concept in object-oriented programming that allow programmers to define custom data types that bundle data and functions together. This unit will cover the basics of defining and using classes in C++.
notes_text: This unit on classes builds on prior knowledge of structs and functions. Classes are the primary mechanism for implementing object-oriented programming in C++, enabling encapsulation, abstraction, and code reuse.

title: Object-Oriented Approach
summary: Introduces the object-oriented approach: modeling software as interacting objects that fuse data and functions, supporting encapsulation and abstraction.
main_text: The object-oriented approach models an application or software system as a set of objects that interact with each other. Objects fuse data (variables) and functions (also known as methods) that operate on that data into one item (an object). Objects replace global-level functions as the primary method of encapsulation and abstraction. Encapsulation means hiding implementation and controlling access. It involves grouping data and the code that operates on that data together into one unit, and only exposing a well-defined interface to control misuse of the code by other programmers. Abstraction refers to hiding data and implementation details. It is how we decompose the problem and think about our design at a higher level rather than considering everything at the lower level.
notes_text: Encapsulation and abstraction are two of the four pillars of object-oriented programming (along with inheritance and polymorphism, covered later). Encapsulation protects internal state from unintended modification, while abstraction lets users work with simplified interfaces without needing to understand the underlying complexity.

title: Object-Oriented Programming: Data Members and Methods
summary: Explains that objects contain data members for state and methods for behavior, using a Deck of cards as a concrete example.
main_text: Objects contain two main components: data members and methods/functions. Data members are the data needed to model the object and track its state or operation, similar to struct fields. Methods or functions are the code that operates on the object, modifies it, and provides behavior. As an example, consider a Deck of cards object. Its data members include an array of 52 entries (one for each card) indicating their ordering, where integers 0 through 51 represent the 52 cards, and a top index tracking the current position. Its methods or functions include shuffle(), cut(int where), and get_top_card(). The slide shows a table mapping array indices 0 through 6 to values 0 through 6, which correspond to cards like 2 of clubs, 2 of spades, 2 of hearts, 2 of diamonds, 3 of clubs, 3 of spades, and 3 of hearts.
notes_text: This example demonstrates how real-world entities can be modeled as objects. The Deck class encapsulates both the card data and the operations you can perform on a deck. The integer representation of cards (0-51) is an implementation detail hidden from the user of the class.

images.description: A table showing how array indices 0-6 map to integer values 0-6, which in turn represent playing cards (2 of clubs through 3 of hearts), demonstrating the integer-to-card mapping scheme.

title: Visualizing What Objects Do
summary: Visualizes an object as having internal state (data members) and functions (buttons) that update state, perform operations, or retrieve results.
main_text: An object has internal state represented by data members and functions that allow you to update the state, perform operations on the object, and retrieve data or results from the object. The slide shows a visualization of a Deck object named d. After declaring 'Deck d;', calls from main() interact with the object through its interface. Calling d.shuffle() triggers the shuffle() function. Calling d.cut(26) passes the value 26 to the cut(int) function. Calling 'int card = d.get_top_card()' retrieves a value from the object. Inside the object, the internal state includes top_index (initialized to 0) and the int cards[52] array containing values 0, 1, through 51. The visualization shows buttons representing the methods and internal storage representing the data members, with the object acting like a machine that receives inputs and produces outputs.
notes_text: This 'black box' visualization reinforces the concept of encapsulation. External code interacts with the object only through its public methods (the buttons), while the internal data (cards array and top_index) is hidden inside. The get_top_card() method returns a value (0 in the example) to the caller.

images.description: A 3D box diagram representing the Deck object 'd'. The top surface shows three 'buttons' for shuffle(), cut(int), and get_top_card() methods. Inside the box, top_index stores 0 and cards[52] stores values 0 through 51. Arrows show method calls from main() flowing into the object and get_top_card returning value 0.

title: C++ Classes: Step 1 - Define the Class
summary: Introduces classes as the programming construct for defining objects, showing step 1: defining data members and function/method prototypes.
main_text: Classes are the programming construct used to define objects, their data members, and methods/functions. They are similar in idea to structs. The process involves three steps, and this slide shows the first step: define the class's data members and function/method prototypes. The code example shows a file called cardgame.cpp with a class Deck definition. The class has a public section containing method prototypes: void shuffle(), void cut(int where), and int get_top_card(). The private section contains the data members: int cards[52] and int top_index. The class definition ends with a semicolon after the closing brace.
notes_text: Notice that the class definition separates public and private sections. Public members are accessible from outside the class, while private members can only be accessed from within the class's own member functions. The semicolon after the closing brace of the class definition is required and a common source of compiler errors if forgotten.

images.description: A code snippet showing the Deck class definition in cardgame.cpp with public method prototypes (shuffle, cut, get_top_card) and private data members (cards[52], top_index), labeled as step 1.

title: C++ Classes: Step 2 - Write Member Function Implementations
summary: Shows step 2 of class creation: writing the member function implementations using the scope resolution operator (::).
main_text: This slide continues the three steps for creating C++ classes, now showing step 2: write the function/method implementations. The code example in cardgame.cpp now includes the class definition (step 1) and the member function implementations (step 2). The shuffle function is implemented as 'void Deck::shuffle()' which uses a Fisher-Yates shuffle algorithm: it loops from i=51 down to i>0, generates a random index r = rand() % i, and swaps cards[i] with cards[r]. The get_top_card function is implemented as 'int Deck::get_top_card()' which returns cards[top_index++], returning the current top card and incrementing the index. Key terminology: a Class is the definition or blueprint of an object.
notes_text: The double colon (::) is the scope resolution operator. Writing 'Deck::shuffle()' tells the compiler this function belongs to the Deck class, giving it access to the class's private data members. Without this prefix, the compiler would treat it as a standalone function with no access to cards[] or top_index.

images.description: Code showing the Deck class definition (step 1) and member function implementations (step 2) including Deck::shuffle() with a randomized swap loop and Deck::get_top_card() returning cards[top_index++].

title: C++ Classes: Step 3 - Instantiate and Use Objects
summary: Completes the three-step class process by showing step 3: instantiating objects and calling their methods in main().
main_text: This slide completes the three steps for C++ classes by showing step 3: instantiate/declare object variables and use them by calling their methods. The complete cardgame.cpp now contains: step 1 (class definition with public methods and private data), step 2 (member function implementations), and step 3 (the main application). In main(), a Deck object d is declared, an int array hand[5] is created, then d.shuffle() is called, followed by d.cut(26). A for loop iterates 5 times calling hand[i] = d.get_top_card() to deal 5 cards. Key terminology: a Class is the definition/blueprint of an object. An Object is an instance of the class, representing the actual allocation of memory for that variable.
notes_text: The distinction between class and object is fundamental: the class is like an architectural blueprint, while each object is a house built from that blueprint. Multiple objects can be created from the same class, each with their own independent copy of the data members. When 'Deck d;' executes, memory is allocated for d's cards[52] array and top_index.

images.description: Complete cardgame.cpp code showing all three steps: class definition (1), member function implementations (2), and main() application code (3) that declares a Deck d, shuffles, cuts, and deals 5 cards into a hand array. A small diagram shows the Deck object d with cards and top_index members.

title: Common Class Structure - Split Files
summary: Explains how to split a class across separate header (.h) and source (.cpp) files for reusability and proper compilation.
main_text: It is common to separate a class into separate source code files so it can easily be reused in different applications. The recommended structure involves three files. First, in a header (.h) file (e.g., deck.h), define the class's data members and function/method prototypes, usually in a separate header file. The class must be defined using the syntax: class name { ... };. Second, in a corresponding .cpp file (e.g., deck.cpp), write the member functions/methods. This file includes the header with #include "deck.h". Third, in an application .cpp file (e.g., cardgame.cpp), instantiate/declare object variables and use them by calling their methods. This file also includes #include "deck.h". When compiling at the command line, you must list all .cpp files on the g++ command, for example: g++ deck.cpp cardgame.cpp -o cardgame.
notes_text: Splitting classes into header and implementation files is a best practice in C++. The header file acts as the interface specification, while the .cpp file contains the implementation details. This separation supports the principle of information hiding and allows multiple source files to use the same class without redefining it. The #include directive essentially copies the header file contents into each .cpp file that needs it.

images.description: Three code panels showing the split file structure: deck.h (class definition with public methods and private data, step 1), deck.cpp (includes deck.h, step 2 for method code), and cardgame.cpp (includes deck.h, step 3 for main application using Deck d).

title: Access Specifiers: Public, Private, and Protected
summary: Explains public, private, and protected access specifiers, showing how they enforce encapsulation by controlling what code can access class members.
main_text: Each function or data member can be classified as public, private, or protected. These classifications support encapsulation by ensuring that no other programmer writes code that uses or modifies your object in an unintended way. Private data/method members are INACCESSIBLE to non-member functions of the class, forcing non-members to ONLY utilize the PUBLIC interface. Private members can be called or accessed only by methods/functions that are part of that class. Public members can be called or accessed by any other code. Protected access will be covered later. Everything is private by default in a class, so you must use the public: label to make things visible. The general practice is to make the interface public and the internal workings (the guts) private. The code example shows that attempting to directly access d.cards[0] or d.top_index from main() will not compile because those are private members.
notes_text: Access specifiers are the mechanism that enforces encapsulation in C++. By making data members private, you prevent external code from putting the object into an invalid state. For example, if someone directly set top_index to -1, get_top_card() would access memory out of bounds. The public interface provides controlled, validated access.

images.description: Code showing deck.h with public methods (constructor, destructor, shuffle, cut, get_top_card) and private data members (cards[52], top_index). Cardgame.cpp shows that d.cards[0] = ACE and d.top_index = 5 won't compile because they access private members.

title: Public/Private and Structs vs. Classes
summary: Explains that the only difference between structs and classes in C++ is default access: structs default to public, classes default to private.
main_text: In C++ the ONLY difference between structs and classes is that structs default to public access while classes default to private access. Thus, other code (non-member functions of the class) cannot access private class members directly. The slide shows two code examples side by side. In student.h, the code shows 'class Student {' versus 'struct Student {' and asks what the difference is between these two declarations. The class contains constructors (Student() and Student(string name, int id, double gpa)), a destructor (~Student()), and data members: string name_, int id_, and double gpa_. In grades.cpp, a Student s1 is declared, and then s1.name_ = myname is attempted. This line would cause a compile error if Student is declared as a class (because name_ would be private by default) but would work if Student is declared as a struct (because name_ would be public by default).
notes_text: This is a commonly tested concept. In practice, the convention is to use struct for simple data holders with no behavior (plain old data types) and class for objects that have methods and enforce invariants through encapsulation. Despite being technically interchangeable except for default access, following this convention communicates intent to other programmers.

images.description: Two side-by-side code panels: student.h showing a Student type with constructors, destructor, and data members (name_, id_, gpa_); grades.cpp showing code that directly accesses s1.name_ which compiles with struct but not with class.

title: Constructors and Destructors: Motivation
summary: Motivates the need for constructors to initialize data members and destructors for cleanup when objects are created or destroyed.
main_text: This slide raises the question: what is the initial value of d.cards and d.top_index when a Deck object is declared? When an object comes alive (is created), we need to have appropriate initial values in our data members so that future calls to member functions will work appropriately. Additionally, when an object dies (goes out of scope or is deleted), we may need to perform some cleanup operations. To help with these tasks, C++ provides Constructor (ctor) and Destructor (dtor) functions. The code example shows deck.h with the Deck class containing public methods (shuffle, cut, get_top_card) and private data (int cards[52], int top_index). In cardgame.cpp, when 'Deck d;' is declared, the cards array and top_index contain unknown/garbage values (shown as question marks), highlighting why initialization through a constructor is necessary.
notes_text: Without a constructor, data members of built-in types (like int) contain whatever garbage values happen to be in memory at the time of allocation. This can lead to undefined behavior when methods try to use these uninitialized values. Constructors solve this by guaranteeing a valid initial state.

images.description: Code showing deck.h class definition and cardgame.cpp where Deck d is created. A small diagram of the Deck object shows cards and top_index filled with question marks, indicating uninitialized/garbage values.

title: Constructors and Destructors: Implementation
summary: Details constructor and destructor syntax, behavior, and implementation, showing how constructors initialize state and destructors perform cleanup.
main_text: A Constructor (ctor) is a function of the same name as the class itself (e.g., Deck()). It is called automatically when the object is created, either when declared or when allocated via new. Constructors are used to initialize the object's data members to some desired or known initial state. Constructors return nothing (not even void). A Destructor (dtor) is a function of the same name as the class with a tilde (~) in front (e.g., ~Deck()). It is called automatically when the object goes out of scope or when it is deallocated by delete or when the scope completes. Destructors are used to free/delete any memory allocated by the object or close any open file streams. Destructors also return nothing. The code example shows deck.h declaring Deck() as constructor and ~Deck() as destructor. In deck.cpp, Deck::Deck() sets top_index = 0 and initializes cards[i] = i in a loop for i from 0 to 51. Deck::~Deck() is empty since this class does not need cleanup. In cardgame.cpp, when 'Deck d;' executes, the constructor Deck() is called automatically. When main() returns, ~Deck() is called automatically.
notes_text: Currently the course does not have occasion to use destructors, but they become essential later when classes dynamically allocate memory (using new). The destructor would then use delete to free that memory, preventing memory leaks. Note that Deck::Deck() is NOT the same as Deck() - the first is the member function implementation, the second is just a call.

images.description: Three code panels: deck.h with constructor/destructor prototypes, deck.cpp showing Deck::Deck() initializing top_index to 0 and filling cards array with 0-51, and Deck::~Deck() empty. Cardgame.cpp shows constructor called at declaration and destructor called at return. A small diagram shows the initialized Deck with cards containing 0,1,2,3,4 and top_index = 0.

title: Multiple Constructors and Default Constructor
summary: Explains how classes can have multiple constructors with different argument lists, and defines the default constructor as the one with no arguments.
main_text: A class can have multiple constructors with different argument lists to provide options to client software for how they would like to initialize the object. A constructor with NO ARGUMENTS is known as the DEFAULT constructor. The Student class example in student.h shows two constructors: Student() as the default constructor, and Student(std::string name, int id, double gpa) as an 'initializing' constructor. The class also has a destructor ~Student(), getter methods (get_name(), get_id(), get_gpa()), and setter methods (set_name(), set_id(), set_gpa()). Private data members use a naming convention with trailing underscores: std::string name_, int id_, and double gpa_. This naming decorator makes it obvious to other programmers that the variable is a data member. In student.cpp, Student::Student() sets default values: name_ = 'Jane Doe', id_ = 0, gpa_ = 2.0. Student::Student(string name, int id, double gpa) sets name_ = name, id_ = id, gpa_ = gpa. In the main code, 'Student s1;' calls the default constructor, then uses setter methods to configure values. 'Student s2(myname, 32421, 4.0);' calls the initializing constructor directly.
notes_text: Multiple constructors are an example of function overloading in C++. The compiler determines which constructor to call based on the arguments provided. The trailing underscore convention for member variables (name_, id_, gpa_) is widely used to distinguish data members from local variables and function parameters, preventing naming conflicts.

images.description: Code showing student.h with two constructors, destructor, getters, setters, and private members with underscore naming. Student.cpp shows both constructor implementations. Main code demonstrates calling each constructor type.

title: Writing Member Functions and the Scope Resolution Operator
summary: Explains why the scope resolution operator (::) is needed when implementing member functions and how member functions can call each other.
main_text: The slide asks what is wrong with writing a function 'void f1() { top_index = 0; }' versus 'Deck::Deck() { top_index = 0; }'. The compiler needs to know that a function is a member of a class. To indicate this, include the name of the class followed by '::' (the scope resolution operator) just before the function name. This allows the compiler to check access to private/public variables. Without the scope operator, writing 'int get_top_card()' rather than 'int Deck::get_top_card()' would make the compiler think it is some outside function (not a member of Deck) and thus generate an error when it tries to access data members like cards and top_index. The code example shows deck.cpp with Deck::Deck() initializing top_index and cards, Deck::~Deck() as an empty destructor, and Deck::shuffle() which calls cut() directly. Within shuffle(), cut() is called without the Deck:: prefix because one member function can call another member function directly. Deck::get_top_card() increments top_index and returns cards[top_index-1].
notes_text: The scope resolution operator :: is critical in C++ class implementations. Inside a member function body, you have implicit access to all other members (both data and functions) of the same object. That is why shuffle() can call cut() without any prefix - the compiler already knows it is operating within the context of a Deck object.

images.description: Code comparison showing a non-member function f1() that cannot access top_index versus Deck::Deck() that can. Deck.h and deck.cpp code show proper use of scope resolution operator in all member function implementations. Deck::shuffle() demonstrates calling cut() directly from within a member function.

title: Accessor and Mutator Methods
summary: Introduces accessor (get) and mutator (set) methods for controlled access to private data, and the use of const for read-only methods.
main_text: Define public 'get' (accessor) and 'set' (mutator) functions to let other code access desired private data members in a controlled way. A good practice is to use 'const' after the argument list for functions that DO NOT modify data members. This ensures data members are not altered by the function. The Student class in student.h shows accessor methods declared as const: std::string get_name() const, int get_id() const, and double get_gpa() const. Mutator methods are: void set_name(string s) and void set_gpa(double g). In student.cpp, the implementations are: Student::get_name() const returns name_, Student::get_id() const returns id_, Student::set_name(string s) sets name_ = s, and Student::set_gpa(double g) sets gpa_ = g. In the main application, s1.set_name(myname) sets the name, and name_copy = s1.get_name() retrieves it.
notes_text: The const keyword on accessor methods is more than a convention - it provides a compiler-enforced guarantee that the method will not modify the object's state. This enables the method to be called on const objects and const references, which is important for passing objects by const reference to functions. If you accidentally try to modify a data member in a const method, the compiler will generate an error.

images.description: Code panels showing student.h with const accessor methods (get_name, get_id, get_gpa) and non-const mutator methods (set_name, set_gpa). Student.cpp shows their implementations. Main code demonstrates calling set_name and get_name on a Student object.

title: Calling Member Functions from Outside the Class (1)
summary: Explains how to call member functions from outside the class using the dot operator with the specific object name.
main_text: When outside the class scope (in main() or some outside function), you must precede the member function call with the object name of the specific object that it should operate on, using the dot operator (e.g., d1.shuffle()). The slide shows two Deck objects, d1 and d2, each with their own independent cards[52] array and top_index. Initially both have cards containing 0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7 and top_index = 0. The code in main() declares 'Deck d1, d2;' and 'int hand[5];'. When d1.shuffle() is called, it is not Deck.shuffle() or shuffle(d1) - it must be d1.shuffle(). The call d1.shuffle() indicates the code of shuffle() should be operating implicitly on d1's data members versus d2 or any other Deck object. After shuffling d1, its cards become 41,27,8,39,25,4,11,17 and its top_index becomes 1 after calling get_top_card(). Meanwhile d2 remains unchanged with its original ordered values.
notes_text: Each object is an independent instance with its own copy of all data members. Calling d1.shuffle() only affects d1's cards array and has no effect on d2. This is a key aspect of object-oriented programming: objects maintain their own independent state. The dot operator is how you specify which object's methods and data you want to access.

images.description: Diagram showing two Deck objects d1 and d2 with independent memory. Before shuffle: both have cards 0-7 and top_index 0. After d1.shuffle() and get_top_card(): d1 has shuffled cards (41,27,8,...) with top_index 1, while d2 remains unchanged. Code shows proper dot-operator syntax.

title: Calling Member Functions from Inside the Class
summary: Shows that within a member function, you can call other member functions directly without a preceding object name, as the object is implicit.
main_text: When inside the class scope (within a member function), no preceding object is necessary. Within a member function, you can just call other member functions directly. The example shows poker.cpp with main() declaring 'Deck d1, d2;' and calling d1.shuffle(). In deck.cpp, the Deck::shuffle() function calls cut(26) directly without any object prefix. Since shuffle() was implicitly working on d1's data (because main called d1.shuffle()), the call to cut() inside shuffle() also implicitly operates on d1's data. The annotation explains that d1 is implicitly passed to shuffle(), and since shuffle was implicitly working on d1's data, d1 is again implicitly passed to cut(). After execution, d1's cards show shuffled values (41,27,8,39,25,4,11,17) while d2 remains unchanged with ordered values (0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7). The shuffle implementation includes a Fisher-Yates algorithm using rand() % (52-i) for random indices, swapping cards using a temp variable.
notes_text: Behind the scenes, C++ passes a hidden 'this' pointer to every member function call. When you call d1.shuffle(), the compiler effectively passes &d1 as the 'this' pointer. Inside shuffle(), when cut(26) is called, it is equivalent to this->cut(26), meaning the same object (d1) is used. This implicit passing of the object is what makes member function chaining work.

images.description: Code showing poker.cpp calling d1.shuffle(), with an arrow to deck.cpp where Deck::shuffle() calls cut(26) directly. Annotations explain d1 is implicitly passed to both functions. Memory diagrams show d1 with shuffled cards and d2 unchanged.

title: Big Picture: Data Members as State and Member Functions as Behavior
summary: Summarizes that data members represent persistent object state while member functions modify or compute on that state, with guidelines for design.
main_text: Data members represent the 'state' of the object. State consists of values that need to be remembered or retained across various function calls for the lifetime of the object, enabling it to perform appropriate tasks. Data members should be the information needed by or across multiple member functions (e.g., set then get, add_score then avg_scores()). Member functions modify or perform computation on that state. Input arguments of member functions should be values needed only DURING or FOR that particular function call timeline. The Student class example shows: Student() default constructor, Student(string name, int id) as an initializing constructor, void set_name(std::string n), void add_score(int id, double score), and double avg_scores() const. Private members include std::string name_, int id_, and double scores_[10]. In main(), a Student s1 is created with 'Tommy Trojan' and id 12345, then s1.set_name('CS Sandy') changes the name, s1.add_score(0, 82.5) adds a score, and cout << s1.avg_scores() outputs 82.5.
notes_text: The distinction between what should be a data member versus a function parameter is an important design consideration. If a value needs to persist between method calls (like a student's name or accumulated scores), it belongs as a data member. If a value is only needed for the duration of one method call (like which index to store a score at), it should be a parameter. This principle guides good class design.

images.description: A 3D box diagram representing a Student object s1. The box shows data members: name ('Tommy' then changed to 'CS Sandy'), id (12345), and scores (82.5, -, -). Method calls s1.set_name(), s1.add_score(0, 82.5), and s1.avg_scores() are shown interacting with the box. avg_scores() outputs 82.5.

title: Class Pointers: Declaring and Using with new
summary: Introduces declaring pointers to class types, using the arrow operator (->) to access members, and allocating objects on the heap with new.
main_text: You can declare pointers to class types just like pointers to any other type. Use the -> (arrow) operator to access member functions or data through a pointer. The code example shows a makeDeck() function that returns a Deck pointer. Inside, 'Deck* d1 = new Deck;' allocates a new Deck object on the heap, and the constructor is called. Then d1->shuffle() and d1->cut(26) are called using the arrow operator. The function returns the pointer d1. In main(), 'Deck* myd = makeDeck();' receives the pointer. The for loop calls hand[i] = myd->get_top_card() to deal cards. The diagram shows d1 as a pointer on the stack of makeDeck() containing the address 55512a8, which points to a Deck object on the heap with cards[52] containing {0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7} and top_index = 0.
notes_text: When using new to allocate objects, the constructor is automatically called just as with stack-allocated objects. The key difference is that heap-allocated objects persist beyond the scope in which they were created, so makeDeck() can return a pointer that remains valid. The arrow operator (->) is syntactic sugar for (*ptr).member - it dereferences the pointer and accesses the member in one step.

images.description: A memory diagram showing the stack frame of makeDeck() containing pointer d1 with value 55512a8. An arrow points from d1 to a Deck object on the heap at address 55512a8, containing cards[52] with values 0-7 and top_index = 0.

title: Class Pointers: Using and Deleting Heap Objects
summary: Shows the complete lifecycle of heap-allocated class objects, including using the pointer in main() and calling delete to invoke the destructor.
main_text: This slide continues the class pointers example, showing the state after the Deck has been used. In makeDeck(), 'Deck* d1 = new Deck;' calls the constructor (Ctor called), then d1->shuffle() and d1->cut(26) are called, and the pointer is returned. In main(), 'Deck* myd = makeDeck();' stores the returned pointer. The code calls myd->shuffle() and uses a loop with hand[i] = myd->get_top_card() to deal 5 cards. After use, 'delete myd;' deallocates the heap memory and the destructor (Dtor) is called automatically. The memory diagram shows the stack of main() with myd holding address 55512a8, pointing to the Deck on the heap. After dealing 5 cards, the heap object shows cards with shuffled values (41,27,8,39,25,4,11,17) and top_index = 5. The delete statement frees this heap memory and triggers ~Deck().
notes_text: Failing to call delete on heap-allocated objects causes a memory leak - the memory remains allocated but inaccessible after the pointer goes out of scope. This is one of the primary reasons destructors exist: to ensure proper cleanup when delete is called. Modern C++ recommends using smart pointers (unique_ptr, shared_ptr) to automate this cleanup, but understanding raw pointers and manual memory management is foundational.

images.description: Memory diagram showing main()'s stack with myd pointer (55512a8) pointing to a Deck object on the heap. The heap Deck shows shuffled cards (41,27,8,39,25,4,11,17) and top_index = 5 after dealing cards. Code annotations show Ctor called at new and Dtor called at delete.

title: Exercises
summary: Closing slide directing students to complete in-class exercises to practice the concepts covered in this unit on classes.
main_text: This slide directs students to work on in-class exercises related to the material covered in Unit 3b on Classes. These exercises provide hands-on practice with defining classes, implementing constructors and destructors, using access specifiers, writing member functions with the scope resolution operator, and working with class pointers.
notes_text: In-class exercises are an important opportunity to apply the concepts of class definition, object instantiation, access control, constructors, destructors, and pointer-based object usage covered in this lecture.
